Dandy-Walker syndrome is a congenital brain malformation that occurs when the fourth ventricle, which is located at the base of the brain, becomes enlarged. The enlargement of this ventricle causes the development of a cystic space called the Dandy-Walker cyst. This cyst is surrounded by a layer of tissue called the tentorium, which normally separates the brain from the skull. In some cases, the tentorium may be absent or incomplete, allowing the cyst to extend into the skull. Dandy-Walker syndrome can also cause the cerebellum, which is the part of the brain that controls balance and coordination, to become smaller than normal. Dandy-Walker syndrome is usually diagnosed during infancy or early childhood. Symptoms include developmental delays, problems with balance and coordination, and headaches.

The disease is caused by mutations in genes that encode proteins involved in the maintenance of myelin sheaths around peripheral nerve fibers. It is also known as hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy (HMSN).The most common form of CMT is CMT1, which is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. CMT1 is caused by mutations in the gene encoding for the peripheral myelin protein 22 (PMP22). In CMT1, the PMP22 gene is duplicated, resulting in a duplication of the entire gene. This leads to an excess of PMP22 protein, which interferes with the normal function of the myelin sheath. The second most common form of CMT is CMT2, which is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. CMT2 is caused by mutations in the gene encoding for the peripheral myelin protein 2 (PMP2). In CMT2, the PMP2 gene is deleted, resulting in a deletion of the entire gene. This leads to a deficiency of PMP2 protein, which interferes with the normal function of the myelin sheath.
